title: Bridge2AI: Cell Maps for AI (CM4AI) Data Generation Project
text: Machine learning models show great promise in analyzing the human genome to make predictions, but the inner workings of these models are typically difficult to interpret. To address this challenge, this Bridge2AI data generation project will generate a resource of matched data and tools to enable the creation of "visible" machine learning systems, which are built directly on knowledge maps of cell and tissue architecture.

title: Staphylococcus hominis bacteriocins protect against skin pathogens
text:
The skin surface is populated by many types of bacteria, and some of these commensal species help protect
the skin against pathogens such as methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Our proposed studies
will determine how natural products are employed by commensal bacteria to enable them to outcompete
pathogens and thus benefit skin immunity. This research is relevant to public health because it is expected to
provide the basis for the development of new strategies to treat and/or prevent bacterial infections.

title: Synaptic Organization and Function of Retinal Interneurons and Downstream Visual Pathways
text:
Animals (including humans) must distinguish between retinal image motion caused by their own movements
and that generated by external objects (e.g., predators or prey) to survive. This proposal investigates how a
conserved retinal interneuron—the TH2 amacrine cell—cancels self-motion signals to support object-motion
detection. The findings will deepen our understanding of fundamental visual processes, provide benchmarks
for assessing visual function in disease and therapy, and potentially guide advances in machine vision.

title: Deep Learning to Improve Interpretation of Intrapartum Fetal Monitoring
text: Completion of this work will advance our understanding of state-of-the-art deep learning approaches for time series classification and their potential for improving intrapartum EFM analysis. More accurate detection of true intrapartum fetal acidemia and reduction in “false positives” from EFM interpretation has the potential to prevent over 175,000 unnecessary cesarean deliveries annually in the US alone. This technology has vast implications, potentially improving outcomes for millions of birthing individuals and neonates and transforming obstetric care practices.

title: Dissecting inter-region communication in human organoid models with dual-color optogenetic probes
text:
This proposal aims to tailor design one high-precision optogenetic probing system, based on monolithic
integration of close-packed dual-color LEDs and MEA, to dissect inter-region communication within regionalized
organoid disease models. Specifically, we will investigate if our probes with scalable pixel counts/pitches could
advance organoid disease modeling via tissue-level optogenetic electrophysiology. If successful, our technology
will enable high-precision bi-directional optogenetic control of inter-region circuits and electrophysiology across
multiple regions and depths of the organoids, which cannot be achieved by existing RNA sequencing, 3D
organoid electro-physiology, or cell imaging methods.

title: Engineered culture platforms to uncover synergies between microenvironmental cues in modulating liver zonation
text:
This project will develop a novel microfluidic approach to elucidate the effects of soluble factor gradients,
individually and in controlled combinations, on zonated functions in primary liver cells from rodents and humans
towards determining species-specific effects. Ultimately, our novel devices can be used to investigate the
mechanisms underlying liver zonation, chemical-induced zonated hepatotoxicity, and how zonation is perturbed
in liver diseases, such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and hepatocellular carcinoma.

title: Small-Molecule Penetration and Efflux in Gram-Negative Bacteria
text:
Small-Molecule Penetration and Efflux in Gram-Negative Bacteria
Infections by Gram-negative bacteria pose a growing threat to public health in the U.S. and globally, due to the
intrinsic resistance of these pathogens to many antibiotics. A major obstacle to the development of new
antibiotics to combat these infections is our poor understanding of the structural requirements for small-
molecule drugs to penetrate the Gram-negative cell envelope barrier and to avoid expulsion by efflux pumps.
This multidisciplinary project will address this problem by using a comprehensive experimental and
computational platform to analyze, model, and predict small-molecule penetration and efflux in three Gram-
negative pathogens, thus enabling the development of new Gram-negative antibiotics.

title: High-resolution extended-depth phase-engineered objectives to accelerate spatial 'omics R&D through computational optics
text:
1 Narrative
2 We propose to develop a highly innovative line of 3D microscope objective lenses for accelerated sample image
3 capture in highly multiplexed and live spatial ‘omics studies. Built as interchangeable replacements for
4 standard objective lenses on tens of thousands of spatial ‘omics systems across the U.S., these objective
5 lenses will offer a robust optomechanical design, and novel phase modulation to shape the light emitted from
6 target biomolecules. Paired with GPU accelerated and AI-driven recovery software, these purpose-built objective
7 lenses will enable scientists to study RNA and protein distributions in greater detail without damaging the cell,
8 thus enabling the identification of diverse cell states associated with disease.

title: Cue-101 and TCR-T cell Combinatorial Strategy for HPV+ Head and Neck Cancers
text:
Several challenges exist that limit the realized potential of cell-based therapies in the setting of solid
tumors, including high manufacturing costs, poor intra-tumoral recruitment, and limited expansion of
adoptively transferred cellular products. Utilizing HPV-associated cancers as a model system, we
propose innovative concepts and engineering strategies to facilitate in situ proliferation of adoptively
transferred T cells that can potentially transform our approach to adoptive cell therapies.

title: Role of lactate transporters in pulmonary fibrosis
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it focuses on developing a new and alternative
strategy to treat idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis by targeting lactate metabolism through the inhibition of lactate
transporters. Once the molecular mechanisms mediating the beneficial effects of these drugs have been identi-
fied, there is the potential for a significant advance in therapy for patients with the disease. Thus, the proposed
research is relevant to the NHLBI mission to enable the translation of basic discoveries into clinical practice for
the treatment of heart and lung diseases.

title: Transposon-mediated rewiring of gene regulatory networks
text:
Transposable elements make up over 50% of the human genome and there is growing evidence that the
reactivation of these sequences plays an important role in many human diseases including cancer and
autoimmunity. This proposal will integrate genomic analysis and immunological approaches to advance our
understanding of how these elements impact cellular function in health and disease.

title: Acquisition of a Beckman Biomek i7 Automated Workstation for High-Throughput Screening Core Facility
text:
High-throughput screening (HTS) of large (tens to hundreds of thousands of compounds) chemical
libraries continues to be one of the most commonly employed and effective methods of identifying novel
bioactive compounds for use as drug leads, or as tool molecules to advance research. While HTS
campaigns have conventionally used genetically engineered cell lines that are robust and resistant to
microbial contamination, the use of patient-derived samples provides greater physiological relevance, and
the opportunity to advance personalized medicine, e.g., by testing drug effects in individual tumor samples.
Using the Beckman Biomek i7 with a HEPA hood, to be acquired with this grant, creates a sterile
environment and enables screening campaigns to use patient-derived samples, which is especially critical
when identifying drugs to treat diseases like cancer, metabolic disorders, and other diseases which may
require personalized treatment.

title: Unlocking Natural Killer cell potential to combat breast cancer metastasis
text:
Metastatic disease is the leading cause of breast cancer-related deaths, with more than 42,000 patients
predicted to die from breast cancer this year. T cell-based immunotherapies, which reengage the adaptive
immune system to fight cancer cells, have shown limited success in metastatic breast cancer, and a deeper
understanding of the anti-tumor immune response is essential to expand the scope of immunotherapy in breast
cancer. NK cells are innate immune cells that are critical for eliminating metastatic cells, and we propose to
investigate the mechanisms that enable breast cancer cells to evade NK cell immunosurveillance, with the
long-term goal of providing the preclinical basis for new immune-based therapeutic strategies.

title: Activation of Synovial Lining Fibroblasts in Rheumatoid Arthritis
text:
In rheumatoid arthritis, the synovial lining is hyperplastic and primarily composed of activated fibroblasts that
secrete multiple factors implicated in tissue damage. In this proposal we investigate mechanisms by which these
fibroblasts are activated by components of the inflammatory microenvironment, including cytokines from
infiltrating leukocytes, and how this activation results in their functional specialization. The identification of key,
functionally relevant transcription factors and pathways will facilitate the development of fibroblast-directed
therapeutics.

title: Neuronal ABCA7 loss of function and Alzheimer’s disease
text:
MAYO CLINIC JACKSONVILLE
The ATP-binding cassette transporter A7 (ABCA7) plays an important role in maintaining lipid homeostasis,
while loss of function variants of ABCA7 are strongly associated with the risk for both early-onset and late-
onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Since ABCA7 is abundantly expressed in neurons, we will focus on
dissecting how ABCA7 deficiency influences lipid metabolism, mitochondria properties, and AD-related
phenotypes in neurons using human iPSC models, as well as neuron specific Abca7 knockout mice and
conventional Abca7 knockout mice. Our unique proposal should enable uncovering the novel mechanisms
and therapeutic value of ABCA7-regulated pathways in AD pathogenesis.

title: Molecular changes associated with sleep and circadian disruption in adolescence: relevance to substance use
text: PROJECT 3 Circadian rhythm and sleep disruptions are common during adolescence, a critical neurodevelopmental window. The primary goal of the CARRS Center is to understand how sleep and circadian rhythm traits and environmental disruptions during adolescence lead to increased vulnerability for substance abuse. We predict that a combination of biological and environmental factors contribute to this increased risk. The goal of Project 3 of CARRS is to provide translational studies in both human subjects and rodent models that determine mechanistic details of how circadian rhythm and sleep disruption alter reward circuitry. Data from our first funding cycle (CARRS-1) found that sleep and circadian disruptions led to substantial changes in gene expression and cellular function within cortico-accumbens circuitry. These changes, in turn, likely contribute to increased risk for substance use (SU). In the CARRS renewal (CARRS-2), we plan to continue these studies, extending into an older, higher risk population and delving more deeply into the cellular and molecular mechanisms that underlie these associations. Project 3 will first identify sleep and circadian markers in peripheral biological human samples collected by Project 1. In Aim 1, we will assess genetically-determined circadian traits using fibroblasts collected from hair follicles as well as state-dependent circadian measures using buccal cells. In Aim 2, we will perform proteomics on brain-derived and cell type-specific extracellular vesicles isolated from plasma collected in Project 1. For Aim 1 and Aim 2, we will be employing machine learning algorithms (described in Core C) to integrate the molecular clock measures with measures of reward value, reward circuit function, cognition, and impulsivity so that we can gain a full picture of exactly how these measures line up in individuals, and what factors put someone at greatest risk for SU. In Aim 3 of CARRS-2, we will use rats and state-of-the-art single nucleus RNA-sequencing to delve more deeply into cell type-specific molecular alterations in cortico-accumbens circuitry that are impacted by chronic sleep fragmentation as well as a circadian misalignment. Together, this translational project will help identify both biomarkers and molecular mechanisms of risk for SU.

title: Supporting Cancer Research as a Core-based Scientist by Providing Comprehensive Genetically Engineered Rodent Model Services
text:
Cancer kills the second most people after cardiovascular diseases, and conquering cancer depends on basic
and translational research that often need specialized expertise, sophisticated technologies and instrumentation
unable to be mastered by individual researchers. I am a highly accomplished research specialist and a long-term
technical leader who has made hundreds of genetically engineered mouse models essential for the success of
many cancer research programs led by many cancer investigators. With the support of an NCI R50 grant, I will
develop new mouse, rat and Nile rat genome-editing methodologies and many novel genetic rodent models for
cancer research to help conquering cancer and advance my professional career at the same time.

title: Optimization of peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) processing for robust downstream functional immune cell analysis and correlation with therapeutic efficacy
text:
As conventional tissue-based biomarkers are limited by availability, safety, and patient considerations, and most
current blood-based biomarkers do not accurately assess tumor or immune microenvironment status, there is
an urgent need to develop new biomarkers that not only aid in the choice, but also predict response to
immunotherapy and other anti-cancer treatments. Recent studies suggest that cytotoxic T and natural killer cells
isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), may, if processed appropriately, provide a blood-
based biomarker that could substitute for a routine biopsy and more closely reflect both the systemic and tumor
immune response. The purpose of this proposal is to optimize the processing of these easily attainable blood
samples and demonstrate that under these optimal conditions, they can be utilized as biomarkers and improve
patient-specific treatment choices by predicting outcomes as a surrogate to, as well as complement, the standard
tissue biopsy.

title: Investigating regulatory mechanisms of in vivo transcriptional dynamics
text:
Transcription, the RNA-synthesizing process for gene expression, occurs in episodic “bursts” of activity,
interspersed with periods of inactivity. This transcriptional bursting is crucial for proper tissue development and
maintenance, enabling the balance of dynamically counteracting genes in response to environmental and
physiological changes, yet its regulatory mechanisms remain poorly understood. Our proposed research
elucidating key regulators of context-appropriate Notch signaling-induced transcriptional dynamics will fill the
critical gap in our understanding of dynamics transcriptional regulation during development, disease, and
stress, with the potential to uncover new therapeutic targets for Notch-related diseases, including cancer,
cardiovascular disease, and infertility.

title: Mechanisms Underlying Excitability Regulation of Motoneuron Types in ALS
text:
This proposal is relevant to public health because, while many pathologies of amyotrophic lateral
sclerosis (ALS) have long been studied, effective treatments remain elusive. Abnormalities in motoneuron
excitability remain the most tightly linked to disease pathogenesis, yet both HYPER- and HYPO-excitability
changes have been seen in motoneurons at various disease stages and in multiple lines of ALS mice. The
proposed work will investigate how the under-studied hypo-excitability mechanisms contribute to the
unstable MN environment, in order to fill an important gap in knowledge and verify a novel drug target for
stabilization of motoneuron excitability and prevention of motoneuron death.
